title: Restaurant website checklist for more orders
seoTitle: Restaurant website checklist for more orders | ROAL
description: Use this restaurant website checklist to fix menus, hours, ordering, calls, and mobile basics so customers can reach you fast.
question: What should be on my restaurant website checklist before I send customers there?
answer: Your restaurant website checklist should cover the basics customers call about most: menu, prices, hours, address, parking, phone number, pickup and delivery options, and a clear way to place orders. It should also work well on a phone, load fast, and match what is on Google and your phone line.
summary: You’ll know exactly what to fix on your restaurant website so customers can order, call, and find you without confusion.
intro:
A good restaurant website should answer the same questions your phone rings for all day: menu, hours, address, parking, and how to order. If those things are hard to find, customers call, hang up, or move on.

Use a simple checklist and fix the pages that matter most first. For many independent spots, that means the homepage, menu page, contact page, and order page. It also means making sure your website matches your [Google Business Profile for restaurants](/blog/google-business-profile-restaurant) and the phone number people see there.

sections.h2: What should every restaurant website show first?
sections.body:
Put the basics at the top of the site, not buried in a footer. A customer on their phone should be able to find your menu, hours, address, phone number, and order button in a few seconds.

Here is a practical front-page checklist:
- Restaurant name and logo
- Menu button
- Hours today
- Address with parking note
- Tap-to-call phone number
- Pickup / delivery / dine-in options
- Order now button if you take online orders

Example: if someone is looking for a Friday night pizza pickup, they should not have to scroll through a long story about your family business to find the current specials. Put the useful stuff first. If you have different lunch and dinner hours, make that obvious.

A good phone line on the site also helps. If your number rings to voicemail or a busy signal, customers may leave. ROAL can answer the restaurant’s phone, share hours and menu details, and take pickup and delivery orders from the live menu. That means your website and your phone can work together instead of competing for attention.

sections.h2: Is your menu easy to read, search, and trust?
sections.body:
The menu is usually the most important page on a restaurant website. It should be readable on a phone, easy to scan, and updated when prices change.

Use this menu checklist:
1. Show item names and prices together.
2. Group items by category, like appetizers, pizza, sandwiches, or platters.
3. Add sizes, modifiers, and add-ons where needed.
4. Mark sold-out items clearly and remove them when they return later.
5. Note allergy-sensitive items or ingredients if you already share that information.

A simple example helps. Say your large pie is $28, your toppings are $3 each, and extra cheese is $2. A customer should not have to call just to figure that out. Put that in the menu or in a short FAQ section.

If your menu lives in a PDF, a photo, or a downloaded file, that is still fine if it is readable. ROAL can read menus, prices, hours, and address from public pages, menu PDFs, and menu photos, then build a phone host in about two minutes. It can also take items, sizes, modifiers, and notes from callers, which is useful when your menu has a lot of choices.

sections.h2: Can customers order without getting confused?
sections.body:
Many restaurant websites lose orders because the path from menu to checkout is messy. Keep the order flow short and plain.

Think of it like this:
- Menu page shows what you sell.
- Order button tells people what kind of order they are placing.
- Pickup instructions explain timing and payment.
- Delivery instructions explain zones, fees, or minimums if you use them.

A useful script line on the page is: "Pickup orders are ready when confirmed by phone or online. Please call for special requests." That line sets expectations and reduces back-and-forth.

If you take phone orders, make that visible too. Many guests still prefer to call, especially for large family orders, late-night requests, or changes to a simple meal. ROAL is built for that. It answers the call, quotes a ready time, confirms the order back, collects the caller’s name and phone, and sends a clean ticket to the kitchen screen.

One important limit: it does not take card numbers over the phone. Payment happens at pickup or however your restaurant already takes it. That keeps the site message honest and simple for customers.

sections.h2: Are your hours, address, and phone number correct everywhere?
sections.body:
This is the part that causes the most frustration. A website can look nice and still send customers to the wrong door, the wrong phone number, or the wrong hours.

Check these items together:
- Website hours
- Google Business Profile hours
- Holiday hours
- Address format and suite number
- Map pin location
- Main phone number
- Parking note or pickup entrance note

If your dining room closes at 9 but pickup runs to 10, say that clearly. If your parking is behind the building, say that too. A short line like "Parking in the rear lot off Oak Street" can save a lot of calls.

This matters for call forwarding too. If you use forwarding, confirm the setup with your carrier or phone system and test it with a real call. On many landlines and some carriers, dial *72 plus the forwarding number to forward all calls and *73 to turn it off. On some mobile carriers, **21*number# forwards all calls and ##21# turns it off; **61*number# forwards unanswered calls and **67*number# forwards busy calls. Codes vary, so always confirm with your carrier. If you need a simple place to compare options, see [call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes).

sections.h2: What should you fix for mobile customers and local search?
sections.body:
Most people looking for food are on a phone, not a desktop. Your website should be fast, readable, and easy to tap.

Use this mobile checklist:
- Big buttons for call, menu, and directions
- Text large enough to read without zooming
- No tiny links packed together
- No slow page with huge photos at the top
- Menu that opens cleanly on a phone
- Click-to-call phone number on every page

Then check your local search basics. Your website name, address, and phone number should match what is on your map listing and contact pages. If they do not match, customers get confused and search engines do too. A clean website helps your restaurant show up correctly and makes the call button more useful. For more on that, see [getting your phone number right on Google](/blog/restaurant-phone-number-google) and [the call button on Google Maps and why it matters](/blog/call-button-google-maps-restaurant).

A quick owner test: open your site on your own phone from outside the restaurant. Can you place a takeout order, call the store, and find parking in under one minute? If not, the site needs trimming.

sections.h2: How do you turn your website into fewer missed calls?
sections.body:
A restaurant website should do more than look good. It should help your staff spend less time repeating the same answers.

Start with the questions people ask most:
- What are your hours?
- Where are you located?
- Do you have parking?
- What is on the menu?
- Do you take pickup orders?
- Are you open for reservations or catering?

Put those answers on the site in short language. Example: "Catering requests and allergy-sensitive questions should be called in so our team can review them." That is honest and practical.

If your phone rings while the line is busy, a phone host can help. ROAL answers the restaurant’s phone, shares basic info from your menu and public pages, and passes tricky calls like catering, complaints, allergy-sensitive questions, and manager requests to staff with a summary. Questions it could not answer go to an inbox, and once you answer them, it learns from then on.

If you want a simple way to test whether your website and phone setup are ready, compare the cost of phone help, delivery apps, and order volume with your own numbers. Tools like the [AI phone host cost calculator](/tools/phone-host-cost-calculator) can help you plug in your order count and see what makes sense for your shop.

sections.h2: What should you review before you launch or update the site?
sections.body:
Use a final pass before you publish changes. Small mistakes on a restaurant site can cost you calls and orders.

Final website checklist:
- Menu prices match the real menu
- Hours are current, including holidays
- Address and map pin are correct
- Phone number rings the right line
- Order path is clear on mobile
- Parking or pickup instructions are visible
- Sold-out or seasonal items are current
- Contact page has a real email or call-back method

Here is a simple worked example. Say you get 20 phone orders a week, and the average order is $28. That is $560 in weekly order value, before you consider add-ons or repeat visits. Plug in your own numbers. Even one confusing page or wrong hour can push a customer toward another spot or a delivery app. Delivery apps commonly take roughly 15-30% commission per order, so many owners want more direct orders through their own website and phone.

If you want to test a phone setup before making a change live, you can [build a free test host from your website](/try). ROAL lets you paste a website, Google Maps link, or your restaurant name and city, then test-call it in the browser with no sign-up needed.

takeaways: Your website should put menu, hours, address, and phone number front and center.
Keep prices, hours, and pickup details consistent across your site, Google, and phone line.
Mobile design matters because most customers check restaurant sites on their phones.
A clear website can reduce repetitive calls and help orders move faster.
Use your own numbers when comparing phone orders, delivery apps, and staff time.

faq.q: What are the must-haves on a restaurant website?
faq.a: The must-haves are menu, prices, hours, address, phone number, and a clear way to order. You should also show parking, pickup details, and any reservation or catering info that customers ask for often. Keep the most important items easy to find on a phone.

faq.q: Should my restaurant website have my full menu?
faq.a: Yes, customers expect to see the menu before they call or order. Make it easy to read on mobile, with item names, prices, and categories. If you use a PDF or menu photos, make sure they are current and readable.

faq.q: How do I make my restaurant website better for phone orders?
faq.a: Put a tap-to-call button on every page, keep hours and address visible, and explain how pickup orders work. If your team wants help answering calls, an AI phone host like ROAL can answer the phone, take orders from the live menu, and send tickets to the kitchen screen.

faq.q: What should I check before updating my restaurant website?
faq.a: Check that your hours, address, phone number, and menu prices match your real operation. Test the site on your own phone and make sure the call button works, the menu loads fast, and customers can find directions without hunting for them.
